name: Primary Anetoderma

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Histopathological Criteria for Anetoderma

criteria.description: Presence of well-circumscribed, flaccid, sac-like skin lesions with herniation on palpation
Histopathological evidence of focal loss or fragmentation of elastic fibers in the dermis
Exclusion of secondary causes such as autoimmune diseases, infections, or trauma

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of characteristic clinical lesions plus histopathological confirmation of elastic fiber loss and exclusion of secondary causes
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical supported by skin biopsy; secondary anetoderma must be ruled out.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Flaccid, sac-like, atrophic skin lesions with herniation
Focal loss of elastic fibers in dermis confirmed by histopathology
searchTerms: loss of elastic fibers in skin layer
dermal fiber damage confirmed by biopsy

common.symptomName: Multiple round to oval atrophic macules or papules
searchTerms: round or oval thin skin patches

common.symptomName: Lesions predominantly on trunk, upper arms, and thighs
searchTerms: skin spots mainly on torso and upper limbs
lesions mostly on trunk and thighs
skin changes on arms and legs
skin spots without pain or redness

common.symptomName: Skin laxity or wrinkling over affected areas
searchTerms: loose or wrinkled skin in affected areas
dark or light skin patches after inflammation

occasional.symptomName: Lesion enlargement over months to years
searchTerms: skin spots getting bigger over months
autoimmune symptoms like joint pain or rash
signs of immune system attacking body
secondary bacterial infection of skin spots

rare.symptomName: Systemic symptoms such as low-grade fever or malaise

laboratory: Negative autoimmune serology (ANA, anti-dsDNA) in primary form
imaging: Not routinely indicated; skin ultrasound may show dermal thinning
genetic: No known consistent genetic mutations identified
other: Skin biopsy showing elastolysis with special stains (e.g., Verhoeff-Van Gieson)

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of underlying systemic disease or infection
Histopathology showing elastic fiber loss secondary to inflammation or trauma
Diffuse fine wrinkling rather than localized sac-like lesions
Histology shows mid-dermal elastic fiber loss without herniation
Generalized skin laxity with systemic involvement
Genetic or acquired etiology with widespread elastic fiber abnormalities

redFlags: Signs of secondary infection or ulceration of lesions
references: Bolognia JL, Schaffer JV, Cerroni L. Dermatology. 5th ed. Elsevier; 2018.
Sardana K, Sarkar R. Anetoderma: A review. Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol. 2010;76(5):497-503.
